title: One Step Short of the Harvest, the Study-Abroad Program Was Halted
dek: One hundred and twenty children were sent to study in the United States. Nine years later, about a hundred were called home just as they were about to finish. What stopped them was not a single event, but a chain of reports, inquiries and decisions.

paras.t: Before the recall, Yung Wing applied on behalf of some of the students for admission to American military academies. The answer he got was: "There is no room provided for Chinese students." For a program that sent children abroad to study engineering and naval science, that door opened only a crack.

In 1881, about a hundred students were recalled to China. In their protest to the Zongli Yamen, Yale president Porter and others wrote that the young men had been taken away "just at the time when they were about to reap the most important advantages from their previous studies, and to gather in the rich harvest which their painful and laborious industry had been preparing for them to reap." Taken literally, this was a stop imposed at the moment the investment was about to pay off.

In the first month of the eleventh year of Tongzhi (1872), the Governor-General of Liangjiang, Zeng Guofan, and the Governor-General of Zhili, Li Hongzhang, memorialized the throne to select young boys for study in the United States. Chen Lanbin and Yung Wing were, in the words of the Qing history text, "jointly appointed to manage the students and to reside permanently in America" — that is, the two of them ran the program together and were posted to America on a long-term basis. By Yung Wing's later account, the total number was 120, sent in four installments of thirty, one installment a year; the boys were to be no younger than twelve and no older than fifteen. Parents or guardians had to sign a paper declaring that they were perfectly willing to let their sons or wards go abroad for fifteen years of education, with no turning back. In late summer 1872 the first group of thirty arrived in the United States.

The students moved into American homes and attended American schools. Soon they changed their dress, took part in family worship, Sunday school and church services, and played outdoor sports and ball games. Yung Wing records quarrels with Chen Lanbin over these matters, and the students' expenses were disputed as well. One way to read this: these daily details mattered because under two sets of standards they pointed to opposite conclusions — on one side, adaptation and fitting in; on the other, evidence of "forgetting one's roots."

After the new commissioner, Woo Tsze Tung, took office, he began sending reports to Peking. Everything that follows comes from Yung Wing's retelling: the students played more than they studied; they were indulged and petted by Commissioner Yung; they imitated American students in athletics; they formed secret societies, religious and political; they would not listen to the new commissioner's advice; most of them went to church, attended Sunday schools and had become Christians; and the sooner this educational enterprise was broken up and the students recalled, the better for China. Yung Wing also wrote that the man "was regarded by all his friends as a crank" — but that is Yung Wing's hostile characterization and cannot be taken as an assessment.

Then a censor submitted a memorial. In Yung Wing's telling, this censor took advantage of the strong anti-Chinese prejudices in America to memorialize the government to break up the Mission and recall all the students; the anti-Chinese atmosphere as background likewise comes from Yung Wing's pen. The court first asked Li Hongzhang, who agreed to the recall. Next it asked Chen Lanbin, thought to know best from his own experience; he decided the students had been in America long enough and should return. Woo Tsze Tung called for them to be recalled without delay and closely watched after their return. Yung Wing was ruled out of the consultation altogether. About a hundred students returned to China in 1881.

The protest letter also contains one line that clears its authors of blame: if the students had neglected or forgotten their native language, "we never assumed the duty of instructing them in it, and cannot be held responsible for this neglect." We see the text of this letter only as reprinted in Yung Wing's book.

Keep one specific person in mind: Zhan Tianyou. According to the 1917 Record of Students Returned from America, he first studied at the Shanghai Educational Mission; in the eleventh year of Tongzhi he went to America on a government scholarship; in the fourth year of Guangxu he entered Yale University to study civil engineering; in the seventh year of Guangxu he received a bachelor's degree, was elected to an honorary society and won a mathematics prize; the same year he returned home and first studied at the naval academy of the Fuzhou Shipyard. His posts as chief engineer, assistant engineer and similar titles on the Beijing–Zhangjiakou Railway and other lines did not begin until the fourteenth year of Guangxu. From study to practice there was a gap of seven years.

One structural reason we can confirm is that the power to evaluate and the power to act were separated, and mid-course reporting went through almost a single channel. The students' academic progress was not untraceable — the letter from Porter and others is itself a record from the university side — but the formal opinion reported to Peking came from the commissioner's reports (C-E5), while Yung Wing, who knew the students' daily lives best, was ruled out of the consultation (C-E9). So the indicators used for judgment became whether they had converted to Christianity, whether they had forgotten their roots, and whether they played more than they studied, instead of courses, exams and progress toward degrees.

A second point is the timing. The word "harvest" in the protest letter points to the final stretch of the investment-return curve (C-E10): nine years after the boys were sent out, the fastest group had just earned their degrees. One possible reading is that once the dispute turned into "are these children still our people," checkable academic results were no longer the main issue. But this is the author's inference. The available material cannot show how the decision-makers weighed things at the time, nor whether the conclusion would have differed if Zhan Tianyou and his classmates had graduated two years earlier — this counterfactual too comes from the author.

Modern fictional scenario: a three-year cross-department rotation pilot is two and a half years in. Business units complain that the participants "are not like our people," while the project team says their output is just about to take off. One method worth borrowing: at the launch, spell out which indicators the mid-term review will use and how they are weighted (output, assessments, retention intent), and require the implementing side, the hiring side and the participants all to attend the review, so that reports do not arrive along a single line.

Modern fictional scenario: a team is sent out for training, the participants spend their spare time in industry communities, and some people worry their "minds have scattered." One method worth borrowing is to separate "behavior change" from "capability loss": the first is judged by whether it affects the outputs agreed in advance; the second is argued with checkable certificates, projects and exam results. When writing up review conclusions, state which parts are records and which are impressions.

The account of the recall and its reasons here comes mainly from Yung Wing's 1909 memoir. He was one of the parties involved and was strongly hostile to Chen Lanbin and Woo Tsze Tung. The original text of the Qing court's recall memorial was not obtained for this piece. The identification "Woo Tsze Tung is generally taken to be Wu Zideng" is not directly supported by this evidence packet and can only be listed as background to be verified. The anti-Chinese atmosphere in America is likewise Yung Wing's description, and the text of Porter's protest is known only as reprinted in Yung Wing's book. So on the question "why were they recalled," the available material gives one side's account plus one protest letter — not enough for a settled verdict, and certainly not something to treat as a model of organizational decision-making.

reflection.type: Decision-making under uncertainty (how to assess a program mid-course)
reflection.scenario: A company's three-year data-engineering overseas training program is two and a half years in. The business line head reports that the participants "don't feel like one of us culturally," while the participants are just about to enter core projects.
reflection.question: When reviewing a long-term training program mid-way, if "does it fit the organizational culture" and "when will professional output pay off" point to opposite conclusions, on what evidence should we decide to continue, cut back, or stop? Who is qualified to make that judgment?

example.assumptions: The program's goal is to develop people who can independently take charge of core systems; three years is the agreed term, and two and a half years of process data already exist. The cultural impressions are mostly impressions; the professional output has checkable records.
example.steps: First list the two kinds of indicators separately: checkable output (deliverables, assessments, certificates) and subjective impressions ("are they like us"), scored separately. Have the hiring side, the implementing side and the participants all state their cases at the meeting. Finally, set a clear payoff point and a stop-loss line before deciding whether to continue.
example.alternative: Another reasonable option is to cut back right away and keep only a few people for the last six months: the reason being that the cultural friction has already affected teamwork, and even if the professional output is about to pay off, the organizational cost may be too high. This alternative is proposed by the author.

uncertainty_note: The original text of the recall memorial was not obtained for this piece. The course of and reasons for the recall come mainly from Yung Wing's 1909 memoir; he was one of the parties involved and was strongly hostile to Chen Lanbin and Woo Tsze Tung. The contents of Woo's reports as retold by him, the censor's motives for his memorial, and the anti-Chinese atmosphere in America are all uncorroborated by independent sources. The text of the protest by Porter and others survives only as reprinted in Yung Wing's book; no original has been seen. Woo Tsze Tung is generally taken to be Wu Zideng, but this evidence packet does not directly establish the identification, so it is listed as to be verified. Zhan Tianyou's record comes from the 1917 Record of Students Returned from America, a single source; his 1881 Yale bachelor's degree in civil engineering and his return home the same year are as recorded there (seventh year of Guangxu). The list of disputes between Chen Lanbin and Yung Wing comes from Yung Wing's one-sided account.

background_claims: Era-name conversions: eleventh year of Tongzhi = 1872, fourth year of Guangxu = 1878, seventh year of Guangxu = 1881, fourteenth year of Guangxu = 1888, first year of the Republic = 1912
Woo Tsze Tung is generally taken to be Wu Zideng (not directly established by this evidence packet; to be verified)
Porter refers to the president of Yale (Noah Porter); this piece uses only the common designation "Yale president Porter"

"Chinese Educational Mission students" and "the Educational Mission (Zhuyang Shiye Ju)" are later common names; "West Point," "the Naval Academy at Annapolis" and "the naval academy of the Fuzhou Shipyard" are standard translations and designations
The Qing Historical Events in Their Entirety (Qing Shi Jishi Benmo) was completed in 1914; it is a history in the jishi-benmo form, not contemporary archival material
"Yelu University" means Yale University; the original text of the Record of Students Returned from America reads "Yelu University"
